result: The cryo-EM structure of frog Panx1 (frPanx1-ΔLC) was determined at 3.0 Å resolution using 90,185 particles. The map quality was sufficient for de novo model building for most of the protein, except for disordered regions in the N-terminus, ECL1, and ICL1.
evaluation: Claims C3, C28, and C29 describe the cryo-EM structure determination with appropriate resolution, particle numbers, and map quality assessment. The data processing workflow, FSC curves, and model statistics in Table 1 support these claims. The resolution and map quality are appropriate for the conclusions drawn.

result: Panx1 assembles as a heptameric channel, which is unique among known eukaryotic channels. This differs from previous studies suggesting hexameric assembly, but is supported by cryo-EM data from both truncated and full-length frPanx1 as well as full-length hPanx1.
evaluation: Claims C5, C30, C36, C37, and C38 collectively establish the heptameric assembly through multiple lines of evidence: the structure itself, 2D class averages of full-length frPanx1 showing seven-fold symmetry, and 2D class averages of hPanx1. The authors appropriately address the discrepancy with prior literature (C35) and provide evidence that the heptameric state is not an artifact of truncations.

result: The Panx1 protomer contains four transmembrane helices (TM1-4), two extracellular loops (ECL1 and ECL2), two intracellular loops (ICL1 and ICL2), and an N-terminal loop. The transmembrane arrangement resembles other large-pore channels like connexins, innexins, and LRRC8, but not CALHMs. Structural features in ECL1 and ECL2 are conserved despite limited sequence similarity.
evaluation: Claims C4, C41-C45 describe the protomer architecture and are well-supported by the structural data shown in Figures 1 and 2. The structural comparisons with other channels are appropriate and supported by superposition analyses. The conservation of structural features despite sequence divergence is a valid observation from the structural alignment.

result: The Panx1 intracellular domains are structurally unique compared to other large-pore channels. ICL1 and ICL2 form a bundle of helices contacting the N-terminus, which forms a constriction of the permeation pathway. The first ~10 amino acids of the N-terminus are disordered in the structure.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51 describe unique features of the intracellular domains supported by the structural data. The disorder in the N-terminal region is evident from the map quality and is appropriately noted. The structural uniqueness is supported by comparison with other channels in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

result: The Panx1 permeation pathway spans 104 Å with constrictions formed by the N-terminal loop, Ile58, and Trp74. The narrowest constriction is surrounded by Trp74 on ECL1, which is highly conserved among species.
evaluation: Claims C6, C53-C56 describe the permeation pathway and are supported by the HOLE analysis in Figure 3a-c and sequence conservation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The measurements and structural observations are consistent with the cryo-EM map.

result: Arg75, situated near the tightest constriction, plays a role in anion selectivity of Panx1. Mutagenesis studies show that the Arg75Lys mutant maintains anion selectivity, while Arg75Ala diminishes Cl- selectivity and Arg75Glu reverses selectivity, supporting the role of the positive charge at position 75 in anion selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C7, C58-C66 describe systematic mutagenesis experiments testing the role of Arg75 in ion selectivity. The reversal potential measurements in different ionic conditions (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) provide strong support for the conclusion. The charge-swap experiments (R75K, R75A, R75E) show appropriate controls and logical progression of evidence.

result: Trp74 and Arg75 participate in an inter-subunit cation-π interaction that is key to Panx1 ion selectivity. Mutations at Trp74 (W74R, W74E, W74A, W74F) all disrupt ion selectivity, suggesting that proper positioning of the benzene ring is important. Anion selectivity is only achieved when Trp74 and Arg75 form a cation-π interaction.
evaluation: Claims C67-C73 describe the cation-π interaction between Trp74 and Arg75 based on structural data (C69: ~4 Å distance) and functional validation through mutagenesis. The systematic mutations (charged, uncharged, conservative) provide strong evidence for the mechanism. The structural and functional data converge to support the cation-π interaction model.

result: Residues in the hydrophobic groove formed by ECL1 and ECL2 are important for channel inhibition by carbenoxolone (CBX). Mutations in both ECL1 (from prior work) and ECL2 (Ile247, Val258, Phe262) diminish CBX sensitivity, suggesting CBX acts as an allosteric inhibitor rather than a channel blocker.
evaluation: Claims C8, C82-C87 describe the CBX binding site and mechanism. The structural mapping of previously identified CBX-sensitive residues (C82-C84) combined with new mutagenesis data in ECL2 (C86, Figure 4c) provide converging evidence. The statistical significance is reported (p<0.05) for the ECL2 mutants. The allosteric inhibitor model is supported by both structural and functional data.

result: Frog Panx1 (frPanx1) is 66% identical to human Panx1, displayed high expression and biochemical stability, and was stabilized by truncating the C-terminus by 71 amino acids and removing 24 amino acids from ICL1. The construct (frPanx1-ΔLC) was verified to form a functional pannexin channel by electrophysiology.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 describe the construct design and validation. The sequence identity is verifiable from Figure 1—figure supplement 1, biochemical stability is shown by FSEC and purification data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a-d), and functionality is demonstrated by electrophysiology (Figure 1a-b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2e-f). The approach is well-documented and validated.

result: The heptameric assembly is established by inter-subunit interactions at three locations: ECL1s and the loop between β2 and β3; TM1-TM1 and TM2-TM4 interfaces; and α9 helix with surrounding α3 and α4 helices and the N-terminal loop from the neighboring subunit. The majority of residues mediating these interactions are highly conserved.
evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 describe the molecular basis of heptameric assembly supported by structural analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and sequence conservation in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The identification of three distinct interaction sites is appropriate and well-documented.

result: The Panx1 ECL1 and ECL2 are joined by two conserved disulfide bonds (Cys66-Cys267, Cys84-Cys248). ECL1 contains an alpha-helix that extends toward the central pore and forms an extracellular constriction.
evaluation: Claims C46 and C47 describe structural features of the extracellular loops supported by the cryo-EM structure. The disulfide bonds are clearly resolved in the map, and the alpha-helix in ECL1 is evident in the structural figures.

result: Both cytoplasmic and extracellular entrances of the permeation pathway are mostly basic, suggesting non-permeant cations may be excluded. The region underneath the W74 constriction is highly acidic, supporting the idea that anions may be selected around this area.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 describe electrostatic properties of the pore supported by electrostatic potential calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The observations about basic entrances and acidic region near W74 are consistent with the anion selectivity data, though the mechanistic interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

result: ECL1 and ECL2 interact with each other and form a potential CBX binding pocket.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by the structural data showing the hydrophobic groove between ECL1 and ECL2 (Figure 4a-b) and the functional data showing that mutations in both loops affect CBX sensitivity. The term 'potential' appropriately indicates that direct CBX binding has not been visualized.

result: The deleted residues in ICL-1 (between Gly171 and Lys194) play a minimal role in channel gating. Among 23 deletion constructs tested, all showed voltage-dependent channel activity except when the entire region between Lys155 and Lys194 was removed. Functional constructs were properly assembled into heptamers, and the EM density in this region was weak, indicating conformational flexibility.
evaluation: Claims C113-C117 describe systematic deletion analysis of ICL1. The extensive survey (23 constructs) and functional/biochemical validation (electrophysiology and FSEC) provide strong support for the conclusion that this region is not critical for gating. The weak EM density is consistent with flexibility.

result: The disordered N-terminal residues might play a role in ion permeation or selectivity, and additional ion selectivity or gating regions may exist in the full-length channel. The N-terminus of Panx1 may be mobile and further constrict the permeation pathway, and electrostatic potential along the pore may contribute to ion selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C52, C74-C77 are speculative statements about missing regions and alternative mechanisms. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on analogy to other channels (C75 cites LRRC8 and connexins), they are not directly tested in this study. The speculation is appropriate for a Discussion section but does not constitute a supported result.

result: CBX may inhibit Panx channels by binding between ECL1 and ECL2 and 'locking' the conformation in favor of channel closure. Possible ion selection mechanisms include the cation-π interaction stabilizing inter-subunit interactions to create a favorable electrostatic environment, or tight extracellular domain interactions being necessary to form a selectivity filter in missing regions.
evaluation: Claims C88, C94, and C95 propose mechanistic models that are speculative. While the CBX binding site is well-supported by mutagenesis, the 'locking' mechanism (C88) is not directly demonstrated. The ion selectivity mechanisms (C94, C95) are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental validation. These remain as models to be tested.

result: The functional state of the structure is uncertain. It may represent a closed conformation based on lack of activity at 0 mV and the acidic region near Trp74, but the ~10 Å constriction suggests it could be open. The +GS version shows larger leak currents, and if the N-terminus conformation is compromised during purification, the structure may represent an open state.
evaluation: Claims C96-C101 discuss the functional state of the structure but reach no definitive conclusion. The evidence is contradictory: lack of activity suggests closed (C96), but pore dimensions suggest open (C98). The +GS data (C99) and N-terminal disorder (C101) add complexity. The authors appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty, but it remains unresolved.

result: ECL1 and ECL2 may undergo movement based on conformational changes in TMDs and cytoplasmic domains. The N-terminal and C-terminal domains may interact and potentially form a channel gate on the intracellular side.
evaluation: Claims C103, C104, C111, C112, and C119 are speculative statements about domain movements and gating mechanisms. These are reasonable hypotheses based on the structure and analogy to other channels, but lack direct experimental support. They represent future directions rather than established results.

result: Pannexins are large-pore forming channels with minimal sequence similarity to other channel families, responsible for ATP release and regulation of various physiological processes including apoptosis, blood pressure, and neuropathic pain. Panx1 can be activated by multiple stimuli and has capacity to integrate distinct stimuli into channel activation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C22 provide background information supported by citations to prior literature. These are well-established facts in the field and appropriately cited. This represents accurate summary of prior work rather than new findings from this study.

result: Other large-pore forming channels have different oligomeric states: connexins and LRRC8s are hexameric, innexins and CALHM1 are octameric. Panx1 has been previously characterized as an anion selective channel.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 and C57 cite prior structural and functional work on other channels. These are accurate statements about the literature and provide appropriate context for the novelty of the heptameric Panx1 structure. The citations support these claims.

result: The extracellular loops are important structural motifs for ion selectivity and channel inhibition in Panx1. The structure provides an atomic blueprint for understanding Panx1 function, with Trp74 and Arg75 on ECL1 playing pivotal roles in ion selection.
evaluation: Claims C9, C89-C91, C105, and C118 represent the main conclusions of the paper, synthesizing the structural and functional data. These are well-supported by the convergence of structural analysis, mutagenesis, and electrophysiology data presented throughout the manuscript.

result: Unlike LRRC8A, the positively charged Arg75 does not form a canonical selectivity filter. Instead, Arg75 likely mediates a cation-π interaction with Trp74 in the neighboring subunit, which controls ion selection.
evaluation: Claims C92 and C93 distinguish the Panx1 selectivity mechanism from other anion channels and propose the cation-π interaction model. This is supported by the structural data (distance measurement) and systematic mutagenesis showing that both residues are required and that the interaction geometry is important.

result: Application of CBX to Trp74 mutants potentiates voltage-dependent channel activity, indicating CBX acts as an allosteric inhibitor rather than a channel blocker.
evaluation: Claims C106 and C107 cite prior work (Michalski and Kawate, 2016) showing CBX potentiation of W74 mutants. This prior result, combined with the current structural mapping of the CBX-sensitive residues, supports the allosteric inhibitor model. The citation is appropriate and the interpretation is sound.

result: Roles of the intracellular domain remain elusive. The C-terminal domain has been shown to play important roles in gating, but this study neither confirms nor refutes this mechanism due to the truncation. The disordered N-terminal residues make it challenging to understand their role in channel activity.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 acknowledge limitations of the current structure regarding intracellular domains. This is an honest assessment of what the structure can and cannot reveal. The citation to prior work on the C-terminus (C109) is appropriate.
